answers.displayAnswer: Coherent waves have the same frequency and maintain a stable phase difference over the observation time, allowing a stable interference pattern.
answers.notes: Read-only conceptual standard answer. No input interaction, automatic key, or correctness judging is supplied.

answers.displayAnswer: Interference is the stable pattern of reinforcement and reduction produced when coherent waves overlap.
answers.notes: Read-only conceptual standard answer. No input interaction, automatic key, or correctness judging is supplied.

answers.displayAnswer: The resultant amplitude is greatest when the phase difference at the observation point is $2m\pi$, and least when it is $(2m+1)\pi$, where $m$ is an integer. Complete cancellation at a minimum requires equal amplitudes. For in-phase sources of the same frequency in one uniform medium, these conditions correspond to path differences $m\lambda$ and $(m+\frac12)\lambda$. Otherwise, the initial source phase difference must also be included.
answers.notes: Read-only conceptual standard answer. No input interaction, automatic key, or correctness judging is supplied.

answers.displayAnswer: No. In an ideal nondissipative system, reduction or cancellation by interference does not destroy wave energy or turn it into heat or another form of energy. Superposition changes the spatial energy distribution, with reduced regions accompanied by reinforced regions, while total energy is conserved.

answers.displayAnswer: Each point on a wavefront can be treated as a source of secondary wavelets. After a time interval, their forward envelope forms the new wavefront.
answers.notes: Read-only conceptual standard answer. No input interaction, automatic key, or correctness judging is supplied.

answers.displayAnswer: A standing wave is usually formed by superposing two waves of the same frequency and equal amplitude traveling in opposite directions. Its nodes and antinodes stay fixed, and amplitude depends on position. A traveling-wave pattern moves and carries energy along its direction of propagation; an ideal standing wave has no net time-averaged energy transport in that direction.

answers.displayAnswer: Adjacent nodes are separated by $\lambda/2$, half a wavelength.

answers.displayAnswer: Diffraction is especially noticeable when the relevant size of an obstacle, opening, or slit is comparable to or smaller than the wavelength. It still occurs for much larger sizes, but is usually less prominent relative to geometric propagation.
